title: Plain-language public briefing for Harbor Junction night riders: the five‑minute timetable test explained
description: A short, clear public briefing that explains (1) the specific mismatch found at Harbor Junction (buses leaving before trains that arrived within the published time), (2) the committee’s temporary change — moving the last night‑bus departure at Harbor Junction five minutes later for two weeks only and not changing other stations — (3) exactly what will be measured (dispatchers will log completed transfers and onward delays), and (4) the trial’s limits (Harbor Junction only; signage was discussed but not changed; the review did not test whether a schedule change would improve transfers broadly). The piece should tell riders what to expect during the two weeks and where to look for official follow‑up.
audience: Night commuters who use Harbor Junction, local commuter groups and resident stakeholders, and local news outlets covering transport updates.
rationale: Riders directly affected need to know the concrete problem, the narrow scope of the test, and how success will be judged so they can plan trips and interpret results. The main uncertainty is whether a 5‑minute shift will be sufficient and whether two weeks at one station will produce decisive evidence; the briefing should make those limits explicit to avoid overclaiming.
evidence: Staff observed 17 missed transfers in the four weeks they logged; in 14 cases the bus had already left when a train arriving within its published time reached the platform; logs for the other three show train delays. The committee's explicit first trial is to move the last night bus departure at Harbor Junction five minutes later for two weeks, without changing departures at other stations. Dispatchers will log completed transfers and onward delays before the committee decides whether to retain the change. Better signs were discussed, but the committee set them aside for this trial. The review covers Harbor Junction only and did not test whether a schedule change would improve transfers.

title: Data explainer: what the four‑week logs actually show about missed transfers
description: A focused article breaking down the logged incidents: total missed transfers (17) over the four weeks, the split between buses leaving while trains arrived on time (14) and cases caused by train delays (3), plus a short discussion of the sample size, period and station limitation and what those boundaries mean for interpreting the problem.
audience: Local press, transport advocates, and data‑literate commuters who want a clear accounting of the evidence behind the committee’s action.
rationale: Decision‑makers and the public benefit from transparency about the evidence base. Explaining the counts and limits helps prevent misinterpretation (for example, attributing all misses to bus scheduling) and sets expectations about how persuasive the upcoming trial’s results will be.
evidence: Staff observed 17 missed transfers in the four weeks they logged; in 14 of those cases the bus had already left when a train arriving within its published time reached the platform; logs for the other three show train delays. The review covers Harbor Junction only.

title: Practical rider guide for the two‑week test: how to plan trips and what to watch
description: A short how‑to for riders during the trial: reminder of the published timetable, that the last Harbor Junction night bus departure will run five minutes later for two weeks only, advice to allow extra slack when making late‑night connections, and clear recommendations on where to check for official updates and results (committee briefings). Emphasize what is unknown (whether the change will be kept) and that signage was not changed for the test.
audience: Regular and occasional late‑night Harbor Junction travelers who need actionable guidance over the two‑week trial.
rationale: Practical guidance reduces the immediate inconvenience of missed connections and encourages informed ridership during the trial period. The main uncertainty is whether riders will notice the small timing change and whether additional factors (train delays) will still cause missed connections.
evidence: The committee will move the last night bus departure at Harbor Junction five minutes later for two weeks. Dispatchers will log completed transfers and onward delays before the committee decides whether to retain the change. Better signs were discussed, but the committee set them aside for this trial. The review covers Harbor Junction only.

title: Policy assessment: does the Harbor Junction trial test the right question?
description: An analysis for transport planners and committee members that evaluates the trial design against the problem: whether a two‑week, single‑station, five‑minute change — with signage deferred — can show causation or only provide limited operational signals. Recommend what additional data or follow‑up tests would be needed to generalize findings.
audience: Municipal transport committee members, planners, and technical advisors who will interpret the trial results and set next steps.
rationale: The committee needs to be aware of the trial’s inferential limits so that its decision to retain or roll back the change rests on appropriate evidence. Key uncertainties include short trial length, single‑station scope, and confounding from train delays.
evidence: The review covers Harbor Junction only and did not test whether a schedule change would improve transfers. The committee’s trial is limited to moving the last night bus departure at Harbor Junction five minutes later for two weeks, and better signs were discussed but set aside. Dispatchers will log completed transfers and onward delays before deciding whether to retain the change.

title: Infographic/timeline concept: show the missed‑transfer window and the expected 5‑minute effect
description: A simple visual that maps sample train arrival times and the published bus departure time to show how many transfers fell into the ‘missed’ zone, then overlays the planned 5‑minute later departure to illustrate how those misses might be reduced. Include callouts that note the three cases caused by train delays and the trial’s two‑week scope.
audience: General public, commuters, and local media looking for an easy‑to‑understand depiction of the problem and proposed test.
rationale: A visual makes a timing mismatch immediately comprehensible and prevents misleading textual simplifications. The visualization should explicitly show the evidence and the trial’s limits so readers don’t infer broader fixes that weren’t tested.
evidence: Staff observed 17 missed transfers in four weeks; in 14 cases the bus had left when a train arriving within its published time reached the platform. The committee will move the last night bus departure at Harbor Junction five minutes later for two weeks; the review covers Harbor Junction only and did not test broader schedule changes.

title: Follow‑up story brief: how the committee will judge whether to keep the change
description: An article template that explains the criteria the committee has set: dispatchers will log completed transfers and onward delays during the two‑week trial and the committee will use those logs before deciding whether to retain the schedule change. Note that signage was not changed and that the trial is limited to Harbor Junction.
audience: Local newsrooms and readers who want to track the committee’s decision process and outcomes.
rationale: Readers will want to know what counts as success and when to expect a decision. Making the decision criteria and limits explicit reduces confusion and helps hold the committee accountable for the promised measurements.
evidence: Dispatchers will log completed transfers and onward delays before the committee decides whether to retain the change. Better signs were discussed but set aside for this trial. The committee’s explicit first trial is to move the last night bus departure at Harbor Junction five minutes later for two weeks, and the review covers Harbor Junction only.
